parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. d4
parent.overview: Black counterattacks with 3...Nf6 instead of the quiet 3...Bc5, inviting White to attack f7. White then chooses between the sharp 4.Ng5 and the calm 4.d3 (Modern Bishop's Opening), which are about equally common in the database. After 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Black can recapture 5...Nxd5 into the dangerous Fried Liver (6.Nxf7) or play the accurate Polerio/Chigorin 5...Na5 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6, gambiting a pawn for a lead in development and the initiative; Traxler (4...Bc5) is a wild alternative. After 4.d3 the game is a slow positional Giuoco-style fight with a plan-based middlegame, and 4.d4 (Open) and 4.O-O (Hungarian-ish transposition) are further choices. The root is a crossroads: the sharp Knight Attack and the quiet 4.d3 lines have different characters. Sources describe the opening as more aggressive than the Giuoco Piano, sound for Black, and played by Tal, Spassky, Morozevich and Short.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense
parent.overview: Black strikes at e4 at once with ...d5, and after 2.exd5 chooses between 2...Qxd5 (the 'positional' branch) and 2...Nf6 (the 'tactical' branch). In the main line 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 the queen must move again, usually Qa5 (or Qd6, Qd8), and White gains time; Black answers with ...c6, ...Nf6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4 and ...e6, reaching a solid, Caro-Kann-like c6/e6 structure with free piece play. White's lead in development and space is balanced by Black's sound, easily defended position, so the game is typically a quiet fight where White pushes for a slight edge. Sharp sidelines exist: the Portuguese (3...Bg4 after 2...Nf6 lines), Icelandic Gambit (2...Nf6 3.c4 e6) and the Marshall Gambit with 2...Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 or 3...c6 ideas. It is objectively sound but has never been a mainstream elite weapon, though Carlsen, Anand and Larsen have used it.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Nf3 O-O 6. Be2 e5
parent.overview: Black has allowed White a broad pawn centre (c4, d4, e4) and now contests it with ...e5, the move that defines the Orthodox (Classical) set-up. The main line is 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7, the Mar del Plata, where the centre locks and the game becomes a race on opposite wings: Black reroutes the f6-knight, plays ...f5-f4 and ...g5 against the king, while White plays b4/c5 (or the Bayonet 9.b4) to open the queenside before Black's attack lands. 7.d5 (Petrosian) is a slower, positional alternative in which Black plays ...a5 and ...Na6 first; 7...exd4 and 7...Nbd7 lines are older and calmer; ...c5 at move 6 gives a Benoni-like game. The set-up is learned as a pattern (Black plays nearly the same moves each game) but the timing of the pawn storm and the defence against c5 are hard to get right.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Old Sicilian
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6
parent.overview: 2...Nc6 develops the queen's knight, covers d4 and e5, and keeps both ...d5 and ...e5 available in one move. It is a crossroads: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black picks the Sveshnikov (...Nf6, ...e5), the Accelerated Dragon (...g6) or a Taimanov/Classical set-up, all sharp and heavily theoretical with asymmetrical pawns. White can sidestep that with 3.Bb5 (Rossolimo, aiming for doubled c-pawns and positional pressure) or with quieter third moves. The positions filed under this exact root are only those quieter third moves (3.Bc4, 3.Nc3, 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.b3, 3.c3); the main 3.d4 and 3.Bb5 lines sit in separate named roots.

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5 Be7
parent.overview: Black meets 2.c4 with 2...e6, holding d5 and keeping a secure, compact centre rather than taking the pawn. It is one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4 (s1). The price is the light-squared bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6-pawn and is Black's main strategic problem (s1). The game then usually becomes a manoeuvring fight: White uses the minority attack (b4-b5) in Carlsbad structures or central expansion with e4 or e4-e5 (Botvinnik plan), while Black aims for the freeing ...c5 or ...e5 break, a Lasker-style exchange of pieces, or a bishop fianchetto (s1, s2, s3). Both Wikipedia and Chessable stress that it is extremely sound yet can turn double-edged when both sides pursue their plans (s2). It was the staple of the Alekhine-Capablanca match (s1) and is played from beginner level to world champions (s2).
